speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: TABLING OF ANNUAL REPORTS AND BUDGETS
speechtext:
I wish to inform the house that this afternoon I tabled the annual report of
Canadian National Railways for 1955 and the budget for 1956. I am sure all hon. members will be pleased to know that in its operations last year Canadian National realized a surplus of $10,717,689.
I also tabled this afternoon the annual report for 1955 and the budget for 1956 of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited. The operation last year resulted in a loss of $95,964, which represents an improvement of $532,446 over the result for 1954. May I be permitted to make a brief statement as to the future operations of the company.
After the company had experienced a very disappointing year in 1953, an impression grew that the government had in mind the termination of the company's operations. My predecessor reassured the house on April 12, 1954, that such was not the government's intention, but said that the results of operations would be carefully considered in relation to the usefulness of the service. Following the consideration of the accounts of the company by the sessional committee on railways and shipping last year, a thorough study was made of the prospects of the company.
Hon. members will recall that until the Canadian National service was started the government had found it necessary to grant substantial subsidies to steamship companies to induce them to provide regular service between Canada and the British West Indies. As the subsidized service was not entirely satisfactory, the government decided to inaugurate a service with Canadian ships. During its 27 years of operation, the Canadian National service incurred annual losses from 1929 to 1940, considerably reduced its accumulated deficit between 1941 and 1948, but experienced further losses after 1948. In 1954, the loss was reduced to about one-half the figure for 1953, and in the year just ended the loss has been a very modest one.
The company has taken measures to reduce operating costs and to develop new traffic, and is expected to participate fully in a gradual increase in the volume of trade between Canada and the British West Indies.
It is anticipated that the service will operate at a loss, but it is expected that the deficits will not average much more than $200,000 per annum and there are reasonable prospects that they may be less. The government believes that this is not too high a price to pay for the continuation of dependable steamship service between Canada and

Canadian National Railways the West Indies and for the tangible and intangible benefits for our trade and our relations with the British West Indies.
In the circumstances, the government has decided to continue the Canadian National (West Indies) service for at least five years, at which time the subject will again be reviewed in the light of the experience in the intervening time and of conditions then prevailing.
Mr. Speaker, if I have permission of the house, I would now move:
That the annual reports for 1955 of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited, and the Canadian National Railways securities trust, the auditors' report to parliament in respect of the Canadian National Railways and Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited, and the budgets for 1956 of Canadian National Railways and Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited, tabled this day, be referred to the sessional committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government, together with the following items of estimates for 1956-57:
Vote 454 Prince Edward Island car ferry and terminals deficit, 1956:
Vote 460 North Sydney-Port aux Basques ferry and terminals deficit, 1956;
Vote 466 Maritime Freight Rates Act;
Vote 467 Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited deficit, 1956;
and that the resolution passed by the house on January 26, 1956, referring certain estimates to the committee of supply, be rescinded so far as the said resolution relates to votes 454, 460, 466 and 467.

subtopic: CLIFFORD WILLIAMS
CLIFFORD WILLIAMS
speechtext:
1.	What consideration has the remission service given under the Ticket of Leave Act to the case of Clifford Williams?
2.	Is it a principle followed in recommending ticket of leave that the convicted person should have served one-half of his sentence? If so. on what basis has this principle been established?
3.	Is it considered that Williams is rehabilitated to the point where he could now safely be released on ticket of leave with the prospect of leading a useful and orderly life? If not, what steps are being taken to rehabilitate this young man so that he will not be doomed to spend 28 unproductive years in prison?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CLIFFORD WILLIAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to deal first with the second question asked by the hon. member for Kamloops, namely whether it is a principle followed in recommending ticket of leave that the convicted person should have served one-half of his sentence and, if so, on what basis this principle has been established.
For many years the remission service of the Department of Justice has followed a rule of general application that requires at least one-half of a sentence of imprisonment to be served before an inmate of a penal institution becomes eligible to be considered for release on ticket of leave, that is, on parole. I am not aware of any parole authority in any country that does not have a rule similar, in principle, to the half-time rule applied by the remission service in Canada.
The proportion of the sentence that must be served varies from country to country, but in every instance the general rule is that some minimum period is required to be served. The rule is applied to the general run of cases in which the sentence of imprisonment imposed by the court is not more than is adequate as punishment for the offence nor more than is required for the reformation and rehabilitation of the convicted person as a result of the treatment that he receives in the institution. Exceptions are, of course, made to the rule in cases such as the Williams case. Those are cases involving very long sentences where after a reasonable period of imprisonment, having regard to the circumstances of the offence, the inmate has shown evidence of reform sufficient to justify the granting of parole to him. I emphasize the fact that in these cases the rule is not applied. Indeed, 6 to 12 per cent of all paroles are granted before the inmates concerned have served half of their sentences.

The half-time rule is well known to the courts, the police, prison officials and inmates. The rule is designed primarily, in the cases where it applies, to ensure some degree of equality of treatment as between inmates. In the cases where it is applicable it does remove uncertainty from the mind of the inmate concerning the time when he may expect to be considered for release on parole and thus helps him to accept the reality of his sentence. If no such rule existed an inmate might during the early part of his sentence continually build false hopes for early release only to have those hopes dashed when he was not released as soon as he expected to be. Such a state of affairs would impede rather than promote his reform and rehabilitation. Moreover, the rule makes possible a minimum period during which the officers in the institution can plan and carry out a proper program of treatment and training for the inmate. Again, it furnishes to the courts and law enforcement authorities generally some assurance that a reasonable proportion of the sentence imposed by the court will be served by the convicted person and that, thereby, the deterrent value of the sentence will be preserved.
In administering the Ticket of Leave Act the remission service of the Department of Justice does not purport either to fulfil or to interfere with any function that should, under our system of law, be performed by the courts. The release of a person on ticket of leave, that is, on parole, is not an interference with the sentence imposed by the court but is, rather, a step designed to assist in the rehabilitation of the offender in society.
The first and third questions relate to a particular case in which the remission service of the Department of Justice is interested. It is the case of Clifford Williams, now an inmate of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary.
To answer these questions in the sense in which they are framed would necessarily involve a discussion of the merits of the case and disclosure of the contents of confidential reports that have been received in the department concerning it. Hon. members will realize, of course, that confidential reports concerning the background and the development in the penal institution of every inmate are received from a great many sources.
Since the Ticket of Leave Act was first enacted in 1899 it has been the invariable practice of my predecessors to avoid discussion in this house of the merits of individual cases of persons undergoing imprisonment.
Without going in any way into the merits of this particular case, may I say that the latest occasion on which the case of Clifford Williams was placed before the Solicitor 67509-134
Questions
General, who has charge of these matters, was October, 1955. At that time, after a careful review of all the reports, he was unable to recommend that Williams be granted parole. This was not the first occasion when my colleague considered the case. A sentence of 28 years upon conviction for the first time is not a usual sentence in Canada and its length itself was sufficient to ensure that the case would not be dealt with on any routine basis and that no arbitrary rules would be applied that would result in the confinement of Williams in the institution for a period that in all the circumstances is not warranted.
I do not propose to express any opinion on the question whether it is considered that Williams is now rehabilitated to the point where he could safely be released on ticket of leave with the prospect of leading a useful and orderly life. To do so would necessarily involve a discussion of the merits of the case and disclosure of the contents of some, at least, of the confidential reports that have been received concerning the case. As to the steps that are being taken to rehabilitate this young man so that he will not be doomed to spend 28 unproductive years in prison, I may say that the officers of the penitentiary have given and will continue to give to him the treatment and training that are appropriate to the circumstances of the case and his willingness to respond. There are in the institution concerned rehabilitative facilities from which every inmate may derive benefit and, in all fairness to this young man, I feel that I should say there is no indication that he is unwilling to avail himself of these facilities.

speechtext:
1.	Is the Department of National Health and Welfare conducting a survey amongst civil servants in Ottawa to ascertain whether or not the said civil servants are eating adequate breakfasts?
2.	If so, what are the results of such survey?
3.	What steps are being taken with respect to any inadequacies disclosed by such a survey?
4.	Will the benefits resulting from this survey be published?
5.	Has the department conducted any survey amongst old age pensioners, in any city in Canada, to ascertain whether or not the said old age pensioners are eating (a) adequate breakfasts; (b) adequate meals at any time?
6.	If so, what are the results of such survey?
7.	What steps are being taken with respect to any inadequacies disclosed by such a survey?
8.	If no survey amongst old age pensioners has yet been made, will consideration be given to the conducting of such a survey in several cities at an early date?

subtopic: CIVIL SERVANTS, OLD AGE PENSIONERS
speechtext:
This question consists of eight parts. The answer to part 1 is that a

Questions
survey of the breakfast habits of approximately 20 p,er cent of civil servants in Ottawa was conducted from January to May, 1955.
Part 2: Of those employees surveyed it was found that 75 per cent ate a breakfast which conformed to recommended health practices; 16 per cent ate a breakfast definitely below recommended health practices; and 9 per cent ate no breakfast.
In answer to parts 3 and 4, I would say that in each building in which the survey was conducted the results were publicized and the fundamentals of a good breakfast as well as the reasons for eating a good breakfast were explained. The nursing counsellors of the civil service health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare gave particular emphasis to good breakfast habits in all subsequent interviews and are continuing their program of health education.
The answers to parts 5, 6 and 7 are no.
The answer to part 8 is that assistance has been given and will continue to be available to provincial groups of various kinds who are conducting surveys, including some surveys on older Canadians.

1.	Have any representations been received for a national cenotaph to honour Canada's fallen of all wars?
2.	If so, from whom, and what consideration has the government given to this suggestion?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question seeks to find out whether representations have been received by the government regarding a national cenotaph to honour Canada's fallen of all wars. I must say that such representations have been received from time to time from various veterans' organizations. More specifically, the dominion executive council of the Canadian Legion, in its annual brief presented to the cabinet on November 10 last, recommended that such a national cenotaph be erected. However, prior to that time, the cabinet had authorized the establishment of an advisory committee to consider and report to me on various matters including the choice of a repository for the world war II book of remembrance. This committee was composed of representatives of government departments concerned as well as the chairman of the federal district commission, representatives of the Canadian Legion and of the national council of veterans' associations in Canada, and the contracting artist for the book of remembrance.
Following the presentation of the Legion's brief, the committee was also asked to make a recommendation regarding the construction of a national cenotaph. The committee

submitted its report a short time ago, and it is receiving the attention of the government at the present time. I propose to make a statement on this matter at an early date.

1.	Was Fay Elizabeth Spalding, a British subject, bora in Australia, refused admission to Canada and/or ordered deported in April, 1955?
2.	Was she in that same month required by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to post a cash bond in the sum of $1,000 and to surrender her passport?
3.	Was the deportation order subsequently quashed in the supreme court of British Columbia in April, 1955? If so, has the department yet paid the applicant her taxed costs of that action, and if so, when?
4.	Did the Department of Citizenship and Immigration then appeal to the court of appeal of British Columbia and receive a judgment dismissing the appeal in July, 1955? If so, has the department yet paid the respondent her taxed costs of that appeal, and if so, when?
5.	Has the time for appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada expired, and if so, when?
6.	Has the department yet refunded the $1,000 cash or returned the passport, and if so, when?

Mr. Speaker, on an earlier occasion, when the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) asked a question about an individual immigration case, I raised a point of order, and I think perhaps an additional point of order might be raised in this case, in that the question appears to transgress the rule that questions are to elicit information and not to give it to the house. In view of the fact that this question deals with a case which has been before the courts, about which there has been a great deal of interest and about which there are some points of law involved, I think perhaps, with your permission, I might answer it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Let us perhaps go further into the point of order. I have not had a chance to peruse the question, but it seems to me that if through this medium we are going to ask questions about every case that goes through the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, where there are perhaps over 100,000 cases dealt with, we are going to have to enlarge the order paper. Is this case considered to be of urgent importance, or is it not one that could wait until the estimates of the department are discussed?
No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Kamloops explain?

As you will see on reading the question, this is a very unusual case, and the circumstances surrounding it are unusual in that nearly a year ago the person concerned was required to post-I suggest, quite wrongly -a cash bond in the sum of $1,000. Her case

has been heard in the supreme court of British Columbia and the court of appeal of British Columbia, and a judgment favourable to her rendered in both courts. I believe the time for appeal to the supreme court has expired and I am informed that neither has the cash bail been returned nor have her taxed costs in any of the courts been paid. I understand there are some further developments in this case in recent days about which I hoped to have the opportunity of asking a supplementary question today. This is far from being a routine case. It is one of those cases which I think reveals in its clearest light the improper conduct of the department.
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not know how many unusual cases of this kind there may be. The hon. member says this is one unusual case. In his view there may be thousands of unusual cases. I am glad that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration raised the point.
May I be permitted-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will allow the minister to answer the question, as he was prepared to do, but I am glad he raised the point because I think that in future I will be more careful with respect to such questions.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, March 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur):
That a special committee be appointed to examine into the role of government in the field of nonmilitary research in Canada, including:
(a)	operations in the field of atomic energy,
(b)	operations of the national research council.
That the committee be empowered to sit during
the sittings of the house and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee and to report from time to time; and that notwithstanding standing order No. 67 the committee shall consist of 20 members-
*-and the amendment thereto of Mr. Green.

subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) for several years has been urging the government to set up a committee of parliament to investigate the results which might reasonably be expected to accrue from a greatly expanded program of research in this country. He and other hon. members in this party have strongly urged the government to empower this committee to call outside witnesses with particular knowledge and experience in these matters so that the committee might gain the kind of information which would be necessary for putting forward to the government useful recommendations for future action. The committee which the government is proposing today does not permit the calling of such outside witnesses. It will permit only the calling of government employees before it, and as the large government majority on the committee can be counted upon to endorse whatever the government has or has not done in matters of research, this committee will amount to nothing more or less than a whitewash committee.
Because of the limitations which have been placed upon it, this committee is denied the means of obtaining the information necessary to reach constructive and useful conclusions, and that is the reason for the amendment which is presently before the house.
One of the reasons why a research committee with power to call outside witnesses with particular knowledge and experience in these matters is so urgently needed is that this country is today steadily dropping behind its industrial competitors in manufacturing progress. This fact was most recently driven home by the latest monthly bulletin of statistics produced by the United Nations in January last and shown on page 12 of that report. These figures, Mr. Speaker, show the percentage increase in manufacturing production which has been made by the leading industrial nations of the world during the six-year

Committee on Atomic Energy
period from 1948 to 1954, the latest year for which comparative figures are available. These percentage increases are as follows: Japan, 230 per cent; West Germany, 205 per cent; France, 38 per cent; India, 36 per cent; United Kingdom, 33 per cent; Belgium, 25 per cent; United States, 22 per cent; Canada, 17 per cent. The average percentage increase for the whole world, excluding the U.S.S.R. and communist Europe, was 39 per cent. Thus we see, Mr. Speaker, that the percentage increase which Canada made in manufacturing progress during the six years for which comparative figures are available is considerably less than that made by each of its industrial competitors.
Now, why should that be the case? We have a perfect right to ask why that should be so; why a country such as Canada with all its natural attributes, raw material, power and the other facilities which it has at its disposal should trail so markedly behind all its industrial competitors. The reason is that in order to make manufacturing progress you have to make sales, and today our products are losing out to products manufactured in other countries because of price or design or both.
One of the steps which we can take to improve our competitive position and to accelerate our industrial expansion is to follow the example of our more successful competitors. They have made full use of greatly expanded research to develop new and better products, new and better designs and more efficient methods of production.
In order to encourage industrial firms to undertake a great deal more industrial research than they are doing at the present time, I think Canada would do well to follow the example of Great Britain, whose percentage increase in manufacturing during the past six years has been double that of Canada. The deductions for tax purposes which are allowed by the British government are as follows, and I will quote from the information given me a few days ago by the United Kingdom information office:
The United Kingdom-Deductions allowed.
1.	Current expenditures.
(a)	All current expenditures on scientific research related to that trade and directly undertaken by the taxpayer or on his behalf.
(b)	Sums paid to any scientific research association, approved for the purpose of research by the committee of the Privy Council for scientific and industrial research.
(c)	Sums paid to university, college, research institute or other similar institution approved by the research council.
2.	Capital expenditures.
(a)	Expenditures of a capital nature incurred on scientific research related to that trade and directly undertaken by the taxpayer or on his behalf.
(b)	Expenditures of a capital nature on research undertaken by the taxpayer or on his behalf and thereafter sets up and commences a trade connected with that research.
The report goes on to say:
In the United Kingdom there is a committee of the privy council for scientific and industrial research, a medical research council established under the committee of the privy council for medical research, and an agricultural research council under the committee of the privy council for agricultural research.
In any question of dispute as to what claims for allowances constitute research, the commissioners of inland revenue shall refer the question to the appropriate research council listed above for decision, and the decision of the council shall be final.
Thus we see that in Great Britain all expenditures for research, whether they be current or capital expenditures, are allowed as deductions for tax purposes. In this way, all industrial firms have every possible incentive to improve their competitive position by undertaking greatly expanded industrial research. The results have been clearly demonstrated by the manufacturing progress they have made, and by the industrial expansion which has taken place in that country.
In Canada the government has taken a far less generous attitude toward allowing deductions for tax purposes. I will quote the regulations in force in this country today, which are as follows:
Not more than 5 per cent of the taxable income of the taxpayer for the year preceding the taxation year may be deducted unless the research program in respect of which the expenditures were made has received the approval of the Minister of National Revenue, after he has, if he considers it necessary, obtained the advice of the national research council, that is, the honorary advisory council for scientific and industrial research as constituted by the Research Council Act.
Thus we see that a Canadian firm which wants to start an industrial research program which may cost in excess of 5 per cent of its taxable income for the previous year, may have to wait until half the current year is over before it knows the decision of the minister, and then, of course, that decision may be an unfavourable one. Decisions to undertake research programs must be made well in advance of the beginning of a year. A firm simply cannot wait until the previous year's figures have been audited and then subjected to the red tape of the Department of National Revenue for a decision.
Another factor which militates against a firm undertaking an industrial research program in this country under the present tax arrangements is the fact that industrial research is most needed after a bad year, and in a bad year the amount available for tax deductions will be lower. Thus we see that program affecting research in this country is a completely unrealistic one. Instead of encouraging firms that are doing badly to do better by undertaking industrial research, this government, by its taxation program.

Committee on Atomic Energy makes it as difficult as possible, if not completely impossible, for a firm to undertake such a research program.
I believe that this government should encourage firms to undertake greatly expanded research programs, as firms in every other industrial nation in the world have been encouraged to do, by concrete means such as tax inducements of the kind I have just cited as being in effect in Great Britain. I believe that this country should introduce some kind of realistic tax allowance program such as they have in Great Britain and which has in no small degree enabled that country to make double the industrial expansion and progress which this country has made during the past six years.
If it will do so it will be taking a very important step forward in accelerating industrial progress and expansion in this country; the kind of industrial progress and expansion which this country should expect when we think of the almost unbelievable raw materials, sources of power, and every other advantage which the country has. That is the way to stop this country being largely a hewer of wood and a drawer of water, and enable it to become one of the really great industrial nations of the world.
In conclusion I would again urge strongly that this government should permit the powers of the committee which is being set up under this motion, to be extended so that outside witnesses with particular knowledge and experience in these matters may be called before the committee, to give the information which will be needed if the committee is to make worth-while and useful recommendations to the government for future and much needed action in this important field.

subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group are prepared and pleased to support the resolution now before us that a special committee be appointed to examine into the role of government in the field of non-military research in Canada, including operations in the field of atomic energy and operations of the national research council. There is no doubt that, in addition to the role of government in the field of atomic research, corporations have a useful role to play. I listened most carefully to the suggestions made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees), but it seems to me that almost all of his remarks were directed, not particularly to the role of government in the field of atomic energy research but rather to how the government by various policies could assist corporations in carrying on their own research.
Of course that is one aspect that is important and which should be considered, but


I believe the government should be careful in granting further concessions of the nature suggested without at the same time giving consideration to what the final results on the economy will be of promoting that type of research rather than the type of research being carried on by the national research council. It is all very well to say that the government by taxation credits or taxation policies should promote private research, but at the same time it should be remembered that by doing so those corporations which develop new inventions may be able, because of our patent policies, to create for themselves a monopoly from which they will get large profits and returns over the years to come. While the encouragement of such research may be advisable, I think other safeguards should be thoroughly considered.
I am sure that the members of this committee will approach this problem with open minds. The members of the various parties in this house view the general role of government in business or the role of government in research in ways that are well known. The Liberal party, the Conservative party and the Social Credit party say that they would like to see the role of government kept to the very minimum. Their emphasis has always been that the government should get out of the business field and, I take it also, out of the research field if they are going to be completely consistent, in so far as it may be possible.
On the other hand, we believe that the government has a useful role to play in this field. We should bear in mind that the original development of atomic energy which resulted in the explosion of the first atomic bomb was brought about mainly, not through the efforts of private corporations or individuals but because governments accepted the important role of leadership in this field and were able to acquire the services of scientists who were experts in this field. By placing national resources at their disposal they were able to develop the first atomic bomb. I believe that the future will show that the government has an important role to play in the field of peacetime research and that we should not hand this field over to private corporations. Rather the government and the members of this committee should consider the advisability of extended government activity in this regard.
Personally I can see no reason why this committee should be confined to considering the role of government in the field of nonmilitary research in Canada. Of course, I would not want anything to be produced before that committee which could be termed classified material, but it seems to me that in

large measure atomic information with regard to military equipment is public and such information might well be made available to the members of the committee. If the members of this committee are going to assess the role of government in this whole field they should be given every facility to inquire into all aspects of atomic energy research of a non-classified nature.
I have shown my own attitude in that regard when I have questioned the government at various times as to whether they had asked that Canadian observers be given the right to see atomic bomb explosions and hydrogen bomb explosions being conducted by the United States and by the United Kingdom. I can see no reason why the government should not at least give consideration to the advisability of having the public representatives, members of parliament, view some of these tests. If my information is correct, members of congress have had such facilities made available to them in the past. I think it would be valuable information for the members of this committee if those same facilities were extended to them, if that were possible.
I should hope that the government would be prepared to provide all possible information to this committee, that its hands would not be tied, that the government would not try to keep as much information away from the committee as possible but rather would take the attitude that it would facilitate the work of the committee. I hope it would not attempt to give the committee a primer in atomic energy or an elementary class in the development of atomic energy, but rather would lay before the committee the fundamentals of this field so that members of parliament can come to a reasonable conclusion as to the role the government should play in this regard.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron), in his address on this subject on March 1, referred to the great dangers involved for the world in a continuing build-up of background irradiation, as he termed it. He quoted a number of prominent scientists to prove that there was a danger, in their opinion, that a continuing build-up of background atomic irradiation could result in very serious consequences to the human race. In that same regard, I have in my hand a quotation from a book, "The Story of F A O", written by the North American regional representative, Mr. Gove Hambidge. He has this to say on page 98:
According to a recent report by geneticist A. H. Sturtevant of the California Institute of Technology, "the entire human race, present and future'', is risking damage by irradiation from atomic or thermonuclear bombs exploded in current experiments. "There is no possible escape from the 67509-135J
Committee on Atomic Energy conclusion that the bombs already exploded will ultimately result, in future generations, in the production of numerous defective individuals. And every new bomb exploded . . . will result in an increase in this ultimate harvest of defective individuals".
That is a quotation from a prominent scientist. The hon. member for Nanaimo a few days ago quoted other prominent scientists along the same lines. I would suggest that if it is, as these scientists say, a real danger, this committee and the government should consider whether or not the time has now arrived when further hydrogen bomb explosions should be stopped. I myself believe that, with this possible danger to the world as these scientists express it, this committee should inquire into the genetic effects of the build-up of background irradiation to see whether or not the very genetic makeup of the human race is, in fact, imperilled.
Of course, atomic irradiation, if applied in a non-military field, can be very useful. Atomic irradiation is now being used by the national research council. It is being used in important experiments being conducted by the University of Manitoba in the spreading and development of various plants, including potatoes, tomatoes, carnations, apples, lyth-rums and so on. I might say that using atomic irradiation on various plants increases the number of mutations that take place as compared with the number that would take place without irradiation. Mutation is a genetic change that is handed down from one generation to another. So, if a large number of mutations in plants can be brought about, then the scientists can select those plants that show the best characteristics and, by a rigid process of selection, can in a short' time improve the plants with which they are dealing.
I should like to emphasize that most mutations caused by irradiation are detrimental and that only a few beneficial ones occur. When such mutations are applied to human beings, of course, there is no method of selection that we would want to consider. So, if human beings are exposed to irradiation, and changes in the genetic makeup should take place, then, since most of them being detrimental, there would be a general adverse effect on the human race. However, using atomic irradiation for the development of better varieties of grain and other plants can assist mankind very substantially. The report I have in my hand shows that the use of atomic irradiation with selection has resulted in eight new varieties of Montcalm barley being produced in a short time. Montcalm is a malting barley and is in great demand at the present time, but one of its drawbacks in the field is the fact that it has a weak straw. Irradiation applied to Montcalm barley has
2132	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee on Atomic Energy resulted, with rigid selection, in the development of a number of strong-strawed varieties, which should result in increased yield.
That is the way we should like to see atomic energy used, in the main, for the improvement of human welfare by applying it to peacetime uses. The government has had much good work done through the national research council. Last fall I had the privilege of going through the national research council laboratories on the campus of the University of Saskatchewan and I saw some of the very interesting and promising work that is being done in the way of developing boards from straw and in the way of separating protein from grain, the glucose separation process, as it is called, and a great deal of other important work.
I think it would be highly useful and highly desirable if the members of this committee could be given the opportunity to see the work of the national research council at Saskatoon and perhaps also at Halifax. I know from talking to some of the scientists, Dr. G. A. Ledingham and Dr. Burton Craig in particular, that they are most anxious that their facilities and the work of the national research council should be placed before the committee. They felt and I felt also that they were doing valuable work and that the setting up of this committee would result in some public attention being given to that valuable work. I hope the government will consider the advisability of stepping up the grants for the purpose of making atomic energy available to underdeveloped countries. More and more frequently we read reports and statements by prominent people in the western world that we are now beginning to lose the economic battle with the communist world and that unless steps are taken, and taken soon, to make available to underdeveloped nations atomic energy and more of the resources of this continent that are in surplus supply, the U.S.S.R. may fill that need with very drastic results to the free world.
I have in my hand a statement made by Senator William Benton of Connecticut as reported by Marquis Childs in the Washington Post of February 28, 1956. Quoting Senator Benton, the report has this to say in part:
. . . Soviet education . . . system is producing a surplus of engineers and technicians who will be assigned to carry out technical assistance in every uncommitted country of the world.
It goes on to say:
The Soviets are now challenging us frontally at what have historically been two of our strongest points, technology and mass education. The present rate of Russian educational advance is faster than our own, just as their growth rate in industrial production surpasses ours. The gap in total performance is closing. It is closing rapidly.

If that is the case, Canada should lose no time in stepping up the appropriation to be used for making atomic energy available for peaceful uses in underdeveloped nations. I am very glad that $8 million is now being used to provide for part of the cost of an atomic plant for India. I think that is a good thing and I should like to see the government do more along that line. This same article goes on to say:
In two speeches late last year, Admiral Lewis L. Strauss, chairman of the atomic energy commission, sounded an equally grave alarm. He said it was evident the United States was rapidly falling behind Soviet Russia in the training of scientists and technicians with the "certainty that we are turning out less than one-half the number of scientists and engineers we require-an alarming statistic by itself".
If the government is to play a full role in the field of non-military research, then I suggest that very large grants should be made available to assist students to go through our universities so that our supply of scientists and technicians may be ample to meet our own needs and to assist us in playing our full part in making atomic energy available to underdeveloped nations. We are pleased, as I have said, that the national research council is doing a good job. We believe that in many respects the government, through the national research council, should be undertaking more research and placing greater emphasis on this field. I suggest that when the national research council sets its energies to the production of some invention that may be of real benefit to the nation and that invention is achieved, not only is such an invention likely to be of much greater use to Canadians generally than if it is controlled by a private corporation but also the cost of producing such an invention is likely to be very much less than if it is produced in the competitive field.
A few weeks ago I had brought to my attention very forcibly an invention of two scientists of the national research council, Dr. A. Frederick Sirianni and Dr. Ira E. Puddington. The thing that they developed is not a large or heavy gadget. It is something that looks rather insignificant but I suggest that in the future it is likely to be of tremendous value to this nation and other nations in the world. It is a little thing they call a sodium plug. The sodium plug can be placed in the crankcase of an automobile or any ordinary piston engine. After this very cheap and economical plug has been placed in the crankcase of the motor the oil does not have to be changed nearly as frequently as would otherwise be the case.
As a matter of fact, two such plugs were placed in automobiles in September, 1953, and since that time they have been driven

17.000	and 20,000 miles respectively without changing the oil. Was this invention something that cost the country a great deal? I do not think so because these two scientists on the staff of the national research council are not paid large sums of money by way of salary, as we consider large sums of money in these days. According to the public accounts, Dr. Puddington is paid a salary of $11,000 and Dr. Sirianni a salary of $6,600.
Ordinarily one has to change the oil in an automobile every thousand miles or so. If the plug does what these scientists expect it will do, make it possible for the automobile owner to change the oil only once every
20.000	miles, it means that the oil in an average automobile will only have to be changed once a year.

speechtext:
When this committee on research is set up, I think one of the very important problems it will have to consider is the implication of Russia's new industrial offensive. I think all members are quite familiar with the fact that, apparently because of nuclear stalemate, Russia is, to all intents and purposes, embarking on a new development program to further her ultimate aim of world domination. This has come to the attention of editorial writers and prominent people throughout the world. I should like, very briefly, to refer to an article in a prominent periodical known as Newsweek. It is the issue of February 6, 1956. There is a special business section in this magazine which relates to this problem. The article is entitled "Industrial War, Can Russia Win?" It reads:
The clash of giants resounds around the world. Moscow has declared industrial war.
At a time when the U.S. prospers as no nation has before, the soviet union is launching a massive economic offensive. The objective: To destroy capitalism by outproducing its U.S. base, capturing its markets and potential friends in under-developed lands.
Then it goes on:
Close to one billion people in Asia, the Middle East and Africa are likely to throw their weight to the stronger side. On their decision largely depends the outcome of the cold war.
In that same article there are numerous other references showing how Russia has the ability to carry out this offensive to its ultimate conclusion. I think all hon. members realize the vast resources of raw materials available to the Soviet union, the vast resources of people, and also, a most important thing with which I am going to deal at some little length, the fact that the Soviet union has embarked on a program to produce scientists and engineers such as no other country has ever attempted before.
I should like to make a brief reference to this' economic offensive and in doing so to [DOT]quote briefly from this article in Newsweek to which I have referred. It points out, and I will not quote it but merely paraphrase it, that since the second world war, 600 million Asians and Arabs have won political independence from old world colonialism. Now, these same people who have secured their political independence are looking forward to the day of economic independence. These people in the east and in Africa are sick of never having enough to eat; they are

sick of never having enough of what we consider to be the simple essentials of life and what to them are the luxuries. I do not think it is just a question of whether or not these people in the east and in Africa are going to get these things; it is more a question of how they are going to get them. Russia is making an allout attempt to outbid us.
At the present time, in roughly 38 short years from the revolution, Russia has transformed a defeated, semi-feudal society into the world's second mightiest power. Since 1913, shortly before the revolution, Russia's gross national product has increased by more than 10 times. I believe it now amounts to almost that of Germany and Britain put together. This is something we are going to have to face. In order to increase this great potential that Russia has, and in order to make proper use of their resources in both materials and people, she has to have more scientists and engineers. In a broadcast towards the end of last January, Matthew Halton reporting on the well-known radio program on Sunday afternoons, "Capital Report", presented some very disquieting figures. He pointed out that this year the Soviet union will graduate 60,000 engineering students, whereas the United States will graduate 22,000 and Great Britain 3,000. There was no figure available for Canada, but after making some inquiries I understand there would probably be only a few hundred.
Now, the Soviet union undoubtedly is attempting to become the master of the world through science and technology. What is more, apparently last fall a group of very prominent British scientists visited the Soviet union and had an opportunity of talking to their graduates in engineering and examining their education system. According to Mr. Halton, it was their opinion that when you compared these groups in Russia, Britain and the United States, the Russian scientists and engineers were superior to those in the United States and Great Britain. Apparently Sir Winston Churchill referred to this situation as an emergency, and something had to be done about it. It is bad enough to have superiority in the number of engineers and scientists, but much worse when that superiority is in quality as well. Apparently, 1,200,000 students of science generally, including engineers, will graduate in Russia this year, and approximately 900,000 in the United States. These figures are very disturbing, Mr. Speaker. They should be disturbing to all hon. members. It is something that I hope this committee will look into.
The resolution to set up this committee refers particularly to non-military research.

In the modern world of science and technology military and non-military research cannot be basically dissociated. It is also apparent that Russia leads in military research in some fields as well as in non-military. I am going to refer hon. members to an article which appeared in the New York Times of January 29 of this year, by Hanson W. Baldwin. I am not going to read it. If hon. members are interested they may look it up. Mr. Baldwin is a well-known and well respected commentator. He points out that in the field of intercontinental missiles Russia is apparently ahead of the United States and Great Britain.
This business of Russia continuing to develop scientists had a parallel in the past. Hon. members know that before 1914 the government of imperial Germany set up a very extensive plan to make Germany the leading country in the world in science and technology. This was done by the government subsidizing the universities and in other ways. This worked very well, as hon. members know. The calibre of German scientists became a byword. Russia is doing the same thing today, but on a much larger scale. In addition, they have at their disposal not only their own scientific brains but the scientific brains of the Germans taken from East Germany at the end of world war II. They also have the advantage of the scientific brains of a few traitors of the western countries who have gone over to the Soviet.
It is quite apparent that Canada's great resources cannot be developed to the fullest extent without adequate scientists and engineers, and apparently there is a considerable shortage at the present time. I refer briefly to comments by a very noted Canadian which appeared in the Montreal Gazette, of Wednesday, March 7 last. They are the comments of Dr. O. M. Solandt, former chairman of the national research council. I quote briefly from the article:
Scientist Shortage Critical Problem
The shortage of scientists and engineers will be the dominant factor and a critical problem in Canadian scientific and economic development.
In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, Dr. Sidney Smith, president of the University of Toronto, a person whose opinion cannot be brushed lightly aside, has this to say, according to the Montreal Gazette of Wednesday, March 7, 1956:
Industry was warned by a university president today that by continuing to draw off top-notch university professors through high salaries, it may kill the goose that laid the golden eggs.
Dr. Sidney Smith, head of the University of Toronto, said his institution-and others, too-are facing a serious problem in getting sufficient high-calibre instructors to train the increasing number of students required in Canada's economic expansion.
Committee on Atomic Energy
In this same regard there was an article by Henry Eyring, of the University of Utah in the United States, regarding federal support of basic research at a state university. I do not wish to take up the time of the house to read the article. I just wish to point out that Professor Eyring said that universities in the United States are up against the same problem. They have insufficient funds to pay professors, and the professors are going into more lucrative jobs, and there is no one to train the students. Let me quote briefly from this article:
Since the top 10 to 15 per cent of the faculty make the difference between distinction and mediocrity much of a university's quality depends on how long it has been since it last went through the wringer.
There is a great deal more in this article, but I shall not take up the time of the house to read it.
On Thursday, March 8 last, the engineering institute of Canada, a well-known and highly respected organization in this country, and again an organization whose opinions cannot be casually brushed aside, appeared before the Gordon commission and pointed out the serious shortage of engineers in Canada. They also pointed out, as I have done this afternoon, that Russia was training vast numbers. I think that is also very important.
To win the industrial war with the Soviet union we have to develop fully our resourced, and we cannot do that without technicians The Russian economic offensive depends on efforts to build up the economies of the underdeveloped countries of Asia and Africa. They intend to do that by means of technical assistance. This means sending scientists and engineers to those countries, plus outright gifts and loans of material.
I should like to refer briefly to an article which appeared in a newspaper of the capital of Indonesia. As hon. members know, the capital of Indonesia is Djakarta. The name of the newspaper is Pedoman. The quotation reads:
Heavy industry is a magic word to underdeveloped nations. Compared with what Russia has planned to undertake, all FAO and Colombo plan aid fades into insignificance.
That is the opinion of the press of Indonesia. Indonesia is a country which has not decided for either the east or the west. It is in the balance. Apparently the action that Russia is taking is just the thing that is going to make those countries, with vast millions, fall into the Russian orbit. Canada and other western countries-I am referring, of course, only to Canada-must find ways of encouraging and training scientists and

No doubt the boys and girls going through these colleges are able to carry on some research activity at home and are better able to interpret the policies developed by their agricultural colleges.
There are many other matters in connection with which additional research could be carried on, such as the handling of fresh vegetables and fruit, the refrigeration of vegetables, meats and perishable products and the packaging of all types of agricultural products to make them more palatable and attractive to the consuming public. Even in ;he face of our apparent surpluses, I think ;he main question is the possibility of develop-ng means of increasing our production as our copulation increases in order to prevent the lituation which has been mentioned by so nany of our learned men, that before too ong we will be short of food supplies.

It means more fficient ways of pricing and marketing his iroduct. It adds up to a higher standard of iving for the entire community.

speechtext:
Mr. peaker, I doubt very much whether under le terms of reference mentioned by the hon. lember for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) I could 
qualify as even an amateur scientist in so far as my ability to take part in this debate is concerned. I have not even read the pulp magazines to which the hon. member referred. But I do feel that I have considerable responsibility in presuming to speak on a subject of this kind. It seems to me that the terms of reference under which this special committee will operate cover a most important field of activity, one which will affect not only our economic life but perhaps the moral and spiritual values throughout the whole world for hundreds of years to come. In that respect it may plot a course for us which will have far-reaching effects.
I only hope that as a result of setting up this committee we may have a continuing flow of information made available not only to the committee but to the public at large, on the widest possible basis. I hope I will be forgiven if I read briefly from the preface of a book which was sent to me by Dr. R. L. Hearn, an outstanding engineer and head of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario. This preface is by Roger H. Evans, director general of UNESCO and the book is entitled "Nuclear Energy and Its Uses in Peace". The preface reads:
Almost any new discovery in science may be used for good or for evil. It is men who decide, according to their needs of the moment, and according to their moral and philosophical conceptions. With peace now prevailing, with the peoples of every nation eager for the good life, and with ample knowledge now available from 15 years of research, the time is certainly ripe for developing the beneficent and constructive uses of the atom for peace.
And later:
Thus a new era opens. The science of atomic materials and the engineering uses of atomic energy will be shared by all the world. It becomes as important for the public to learn the new facts as it has been to understand the use of coal and steam. The new power will be widely used long before school textbooks can be rewritten and before the children who study them can become adults. An introduction to the new knowledge and to its use in ordinary peaceful living is needed at once.
There is little doubt that this knowledge is needed at once. As I listened to General Gruenther this morning I began to wonder whether we could accomplish all that we would hope to accomplish in this committee if we attempted to keep separate the fields of military and non-military research. In this respect I agree with the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Oxford that it is going to constitute a most serious question. No one here wants to urge that the committee be given classified material, but it is going to be very difficult to make the best use of this committee; it is going to be very difficult to produce the best results in atomic research, if we are going to have it developed on two parallel lines, developed with two separate and distinct groups of scientists,

developed with two separate and distinct votes of government funds, and developed for two separate and distinct purposes.
I think I might be forgiven if I refer again to the problem of development and research in the field of aviation as a typical example of the problem that faces us here. No one can deny that the progress we have made in the commercial aviation field has been tied very definitely to the development of aviation as a means of waging war. The aircraft industry in this country is concerned, I believe it is distressed, because it feels that the government is not prepared to take that one additional step which is required to integrate the benefits that are being produced in military research, by bringing them forward and producing the results that can be produced right within this country in connection with commercial aircraft development.
Now I should like to refer, in connection with this phase of the matter, to the submission made by Avro at Malton to the Gordon commission on economic prospects. I shall read only a few words from this submission:
At the outset, it should be stated that military aviation requirements provide the impetus for practically all aeronautical advances. It is a historical fact that, except for one or two cases, every commercial airliner flying today is a direct offshoot of a military aircraft. The reason for this is that the research and development needed to bring about a major advance are so costly that seldom can they be justified from a purely commercial point of view. This limitation does not apply to the military. When it becomes a matter of survival, economics are secondary.
Further on the submission says:
The use of atomic power in military aircraft also probably is not far off. Its introduction will make a difference mainly in economy of operation and almost unlimited range, rather than in speed and altitude, since atomic energy will be, in effect, a substitute for fuel in already existing power plants. However, until a shielding process can be found which does not involve the tremendous weight of material needed at present, atomic power will be used only in the largest aircraft.
The application of all these advances to civil aviation undoubtedly will depend, as in the past, on how quickly they can be proved reliable enough and economical enough for use in transporting passengers and freight. The nature of the advances will be governed by advances in military aviation.

such terrific commercial advantage of the many millions of dollars being spent on military research in this field.
If we did that, perhaps we would not have the Minister of Defence Production losing so much sleep because he has invested $65 million or some such amount in a plant and is worried because we have not had a single plane in some time off the production line. If it were possible to ensure that the money being spent for that purpose, with the little additional help that might be required, would result in commercial planes for peaceful purposes coming off the same production lines, I think there would be a lot less concern in the country about the amount of money being spent in these activities.
I am wondering whether the Massey commission did not have something like this in mind in its recommendation under the heading, "Scientific Research Under the Federal Government". In that regard it had this to say:
That under the direction of the privy council committee on scientific and1 industrial research, a study be made as soon as possible of all research activities of the federal government, with a view to their adequate co-ordination, the avoidance of any wasteful duplication, and the maximum co-operation that may be possible.
These words certainly fit the terms of reference that are required for this particular committee.
I should like to speak about one or two other phases of the problems that will confront the committee. The other day I received a letter from a constituent of mine who had heard a radio address by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). She wrote me a letter in which she suggested that we should increase our gifts under the Colombo plan. I guess it was a pretty appealing radio address and had an effect. I had to write back and say that I was not exactly sure I could criticize the government in connection with the amount of money it was spending under the plan because after all I knew that whatever help was given had to come out of the taxpayers' pockets, and to a great extent I thought we were near the breaking point in that connection.
But I am wondering whether there is not another answer to such problems, another answer that may be produced before the committee. You know, scientists are able to equate the prosperity of a country or the standard of living of a country with the amount of energy, the amount of fuel that is available in that country. They talk about coal, petroleum, natural gas and even water power, but they lump them all together and talk about energy. They say that using this

formula you can determine just how far a country can go in raising its standard of living. They point out that on an annual basis the United States, which most people agree has the highest standard of living in the world, uses 8 tons of coal or energy, whatever you want to call it, per person; that Britain and Norway use 4-5 tons per person per annum, Japan 1 ton and India -01 ton.
Then they say, compare this with the annual income per person in these countries. The United States figure is $2,000 as against 8 tons, the United Kingdom or Norway $1,000 as against 4-5 tons, Japan maybe $100 and India maybe $50. Their complete standard of living is determined by their ability to produce the energy required for the production of goods used in everyday life.
We are entering an entirely new field now. If we wanted to raise the standard of living of all people throughout the free world to our own living standard we would probably have enough energy of the coal-petroleum type to last us 25 or 30 years, but with the use of new materials, with the use of uranium and thorium as sources of energy, it would be possible for us to raise the standard of living of the peoples of the free world to our own basic standard and keep it there for a thousand years.
Perhaps this is the answer to the problems that face us in a period between peace and war. I do not think anyone believes that merely to complete the building of massive defence forces is going to be the ultimate answer. It seems to me that the one sure way of maintaining peace is to see that there is an exchange of this information, an exchange of the material which creates energy, and the raising of the living standards of substandard nations to our own level.
If we do that we will write the best insurance policy so far as peace is concerned that we can get anywhere. How are we going to do it? First of all we in this house have to get the information, and later we have got to do our part as parliamentarians to see that the information is distributed to the right people and ensure that the basic commercial quantities of the goods we have that will do this job are also made available to them.
I do not see why we cannot have the type of parliamentary and scientific committee they have at Westminster. The committee there can meet regularly. It can call before it scientists of all types. It can bring them from other lands as well. These scientists give lectures on this type of topic, so that every bit of information that is of commercial value is placed right on their doorstep.
Committee on Atomic Energy
If 'we could get such information perhaps we could help to solve some of the problems to which the hon. member for Oxford rereferred, when he mentioned the fact that we were losing out in the educational race. He pointed out that we are not producing the engineers we require to carry on this job. If we did that perhaps we could get away from such headlines as that which appeared in the Toronto Telegram last year, namely, "Lack of Engineers Surprising to Howe." If it is surprising to him, let us get the committee going and find out all about it. Maybe the Minister of Defence Production will be able to learn the answer as to why we do not have the engineers. In the article he is reported as saying:
"This is hard for me to understand", Mr. Howe told the annual dinner of the association of consulting engineers here.
I had a letter from a friend in the United States the other day, and he said it was not very hard for him to understand. In the last three or four years we have had $395 million of engineering work done in this country, and all but approximately $33 million of it was done in the United States and shipped here. Perhaps that is one reason we do not have people with engineering skill remain in this country.
All in all, here is one opportunity. Let us not allow it to slip through our fingers. Surely the amendment which has been proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra places with the committee the power to get the answers, the power to see that the information made available to it is given to the proper people in this country and the proper people in other countries to ensure that we all go forward, as freedom-loving nations, in the development of atomic energy for the use of all mankind and not just for the use of a few.

Today, carved out of the forest, we have one of the finest towns in Canada with a population between 4,000 and 5,000 people. It is composed mostly of brilliant scientists, people who are making a great contribution to the life of our country and to the scientific research which is being conducted at the present time. I deeply regret the passing the other day of Dr. Cipriani at Deep River. He was one of the leading scientists in Canada, perhaps in the world.

Committee on Atomic Energy As I say, no doubt the committee will' have an opportunity of visiting the place where these great developments have occurred during the last four years. As we all know, of course, one of the outstanding developments has been the cobalt bomb, which has been distributed throughout Canada and to many other nations in the world. It has been of great value in the treatment of cancer. These scientists at Deep River are quiet, modest and industrious people who are working away without receiving what I consider to be adequate compensation. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
It gives me great pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to support this resolution at this time because I believe the work of this committee will be a valuable contribution to the development of Canada. We are specifically to inquire into two sections, namely the operations in the field of atomic energy for peacetime purposes and the operations of the national research council. The national research council is an important government bocvy in Canada, and I believe it will be very valuable to examine the operations of that council because I think we will be struck by its accomplishments. The national research council is responsible for co-ordinating all federal government research, I speak particularly of medical research as the Department of National Health and Welfare is very much interested in the development of such research.
I think it is quite evident to all of us that in many fields Canada is taking a lead in research. I propose to discuss at some length research in the field of health and welfare, [Mr. Forgie.l

in which field I believe hon. members will agree that progress has been rapid and accomplishments great.

subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext: In Canada?

subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Very definitely, and I will prove that point as I go along. The need for research in health and welfare matters has been long recognized. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has laid great stress on the need for research in these fields. He has always felt that only by extensive research can we provide the foundation necessary for success in all aspects of health and welfare planning. Research in health matters has been enormously extended in the post war years, and it was during this period that welfare research first began to command serious attention.
Health and welfare research in Canada is now limited by several factors. The first and most important of these is the shortage of trained personnel. There can be no doubt that the most important need is to have well trained and eager scientists who are prepared to give their life to research. I should like also to join with the hon. member who has just taken his seat in paying tribute to Dr. Cipriani, who died a few weeks ago. We in our department know what a splendid contribution he made to medical research in this country. The second limiting factor is financial resources, although when we consider the vast sums which are presently being spent on health and welfare research in Canada this is not of primary importance at the moment. The need for additional financial assistance is probably limited by the lack of trained personnel.
Perhaps our greatest need at the present time is in the professional co-ordination and planning of research so that, as far as possible in this complex field, we direct our work to the most productive field and prevent needless duplication and overlapping. In so far as health research is concerned, all projects supported by the federal government are considered by a co-ordinating committee of technically competent experts before being recommended for approval or rejection to the research advisory committee. The general policy covering all medical research is under constant examination by the privy council committee on scientific and industrial research policy. In welfare research there is close liaison among the Department of National Health and Welfare, the provincial welfare agencies, the Canadian welfare council and other voluntary organizations and the schools of social work.
Let us examine the expenditure on medical research in Canada. Over $7 million is now being spent in Canada in health research. Of

this amount, $4 million comes from federal government sources and the remainder is contributed by universities, charitable organizations, the provinces and commercial organizations.
The federal budget for health research is eight times as large as in 1938, and four times as large as in 1948. In addition to the national health and welfare department, three other federal agencies sponsor programs of medical research; a division of medical research of the national research council, the medical section of the defence research board, and the Department of Veterans Affairs. These four agencies contribute more than half of today's annual expenditures in health research.
Through the national health program, $1-8 million was made available for research in 1954-55. Nearly $8 million has been provided under this program since its commencement in 1948. The percentage of the amount available which has actually been spent has risen from 59 per cent in that year to 88 per cent last year, the average expenditure during the life of the program being 85 per cent of the funds available.
In addition to these funds for specific research projects, $1 million has been provided under this program for technical equipment for research performance. Only a few weeks ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare approved a grant of some $24,000 to the University of Toronto for the purchase of special equipment for the extension of research work on heart disease in the province of Ontario. This grant brought to more than $125,000 the amount of federal assistance for heart research in this province during the current fiscal year. This equipment will be established in the Toronto General hospital under the supervision of the department of medicine and surgery at the university. It is part of a province-wide program for the extension of research and the development of new diagnostic and treatment techniques.

At one stage it was found that in order to grow the poliomyelitis virus, live tissue cells in a culture medium were required. While numerous investigators were engaged in the search for such a medium, a synthetic solution developed in Canada in connection with cancer research, medium 199, proved to be the answer and this combination was used by Salk in the production of poliomyelitis virus.
This not only permitted the original developmental work to progress at a greatly accelerated pace but also paved the way for the production of massive quantities of the vaccine. Further, the research investment at the Connaught laboratories has resulted in the cost of the final product there being much lower, in actual figures about one-third of the cost of the commercially produced vaccine.
Research on the production of ACTH and cortisone at the Connaught medical research laboratories made possible improved and more economical methods for the production of these drugs, so that the cost of the 25 milligram vial, which in 1950 cost $5, was reduced to $1.75 a few years later.
