speechtext:
A few months ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare convened a meeting of leading heart authorities from all parts of Canada, and as a result the Canadian heart foundation was formed. This foundation will have affiliated provincial associations, and its main purpose will be to raise money to carry out basic and clinical research on all heart disease. I am sure it will make the same splendid contribution to research which is being made by the national cancer institute, the Canadian arthritis and rheumatism association, and other similar bodies in Canada.
There are numerous studies being carried out in Canada on arthritis and rheumatism. These studies should contribute materially to the finding of some satisfactory cure for these

Committee on Atomic Energy crippling diseases, which affect some 225,000 Canadians of which number 115,000 are severely or totally disabled.
Time does not allow me to dwell longer on the various research projects being carried on through the federal health grants. Over 400 individual projects have been approved by the minister and are in various stages of completion. Many of these will produce results of profound importance.
Mention should be made, however, of the Canadian sickness survey which was carried out between 1950 and 1951 and involved the study of some 50,000 persons in all age groups and social classes throughout Canada. This survey indicated the nature and extent of sickness among Canadian people, the effect of illness and disability on the population and the health care they received. This survey has been published in detail and has received world-wide recognition for its successful prosecution and productive outcome.
The national health survey was carried out early in the national health program in order to assist the provinces to take an inventory of their health resources. The research and statistics division of the department will shortly publish a comprehensive half-million word report on this survey. Both these reports have been of great value in laying the basis for the health insurance studies which have been going on in the department for some years.
Comprehensive bulletins have been produced on health insurance systems in force in the principle countries of the world, and on our own public non-profit and commercial schemes in Canada.
Extensive analysis of costs and utilization of data have been carried out both by the provinces and the federal government, and this analysis proved of immense value at the recent federal-provincial conference on health insurance. Without them a scientific and responsible approach to the problem of health insurance would have been impossible, and the proposal made by the federal government at this conference for the introduction of health insurance in Canada would have been impossible.
Welfare research has not made the advances that health research has, but a number of important studies have been carried out by the Department of National Health and Welfare. The research done for the old age security committee of this house made possible an intelligent approach to and solution of the old age security problem.
Studies carried out by this department made possible the commencement of the disability allowance program. A survey of welfare


positions in Canada a few years ago indicated the need for increased members of welfare personnel. We have also made studies of the various welfare services in Canada and these have been published in bulletin form for the assistance of welfare planners. Studies have been made for the United Nations and its specialized agencies on various aspects of welfare services in Canada.
I believe this brief outline of the various research activities in the health and welfare field which I have presented proves very definitely that medical research workers are quite well aware of their responsibility and are taking every possible means to improve the quality and quantity of medical research. We can, I think, look forward to gradually unlocking the doors behind which are the secrets of many of the most formidable diseases now afflicting the human race.
I believe that the establishment of this committee and the work it will do will make a further important contribution to medical research in this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this occasion it is possible for me to commence my remarks with the well-worn phrase that I did not intend to take part in this debate. The remarks I shall make will make the truth of that well-worn statement obvious. I have been prompted to take part in this discussion by the very interesting speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Robertson). I am also delighted that a point of order was raised during the course of the hon. member's speech on which Your Honour ruled, making it clear that we are permitted to discuss any phase of nonmilitary research.
I agree with the hon. member for Northumberland as to the important part which has been played in this country by research of the type made possible by the Department of National Health and Welfare. I welcome, as do all hon. members, the medical research which has been carried on by the department or which has been facilitated by federal grants made under the direction of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I agree also with the hon. member that the research which has been carried on by the research division of the Department of National Health and Welfare with regard to health insurance has been extremely valuable. It is still my view that after 37 years of talking about bringing in health insurance the Liberals ought to have plenty of material of their own on which to base such a program. However, it is a fact that the research into this important problem which has been carried on by the department has provided the

basis upon which a national program of health insurance can now be established.
As a matter of fact I am satisfied that the extent of the research which has been carried on would make possible a much bolder step in the field of national health insurance than is envisaged in the proposals made by the federal government to the provinces at the conference held recently in the city of Ottawa. If we are not moving ahead as fast as we should it is not the fault of those who have done the research, it is the fault of the government which is still dragging its feet in this important field.
Likewise I join with the hon. member for Northumberland in expressing thanks to the research division of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the excellent work they did for our committee on old age security which met in 1950. I am sure that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage), who was a joint chairman of that committee, will agree with me that the research done by the department provided the basis on which we were able to make intelligent decisions in the important field of old age security.
It is precisely because of the importance of the groundwork which is done by those who do research that I feel further research should be done into the whole question of how our older people are getting along. There were a few twitters in the house this afternoon when a starred question of mine was called. I refer to the one that asked about civil servants' breakfast habits. There were further twitters when the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare made his reply.
I want to say that I was quite serious in putting that set of questions on the order paper. I was serious with respect to both parts of it. I approve of what the nutrition branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare is doing by way of conducting research into the eating habits of some sections of the Canadian population. I feel that by continuing such research, information can be obtained on the basis of which education can be made available in an effort to improve the health of our people through better nutrition.
I was not only quite serious in my interest in what the nutrition branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare is doing among the Ottawa civil servants, I was also extremely serious in my suggestion that similar surveys might be made among groups of old age pensioners in this country. In fact my question suggested that research might be made not only into the question of whether
Committee on Atomic Energy or not old age pensioners are eating adequate breakfasts, but as to whether or not they are getting adequate meals at any time of the day. Therefore I urge most strongly that the research envisaged in the motion now on the order paper be extended into this whole field of how people of 65 and 70 years of age and over are faring in this wonderful country at this time.
Some days ago I suggested to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that a special committee might be appointed to review all our old age legislation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare in one of those typical responses of his chose to present a question to me rather than to answer my question.
I remind the house now that my request for research into how our older citizens are faring was based on the fact that the welfare council of greater Winnipeg has carried on research into this matter and has produced an interesting report entitled "Age and Opportunity". When I referred to it on February 29 the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated that he had seen a copy of this report, and I hope that in the meantime he has had an opportunity to study it.
I remind the minister and others that in this report are included a number of recommendations. One of them is to the effect that the whole policy of our old age legislation should be reviewed every four or five years. The welfare council points out that this was the recommendation of the Canadian Welfare Council when it appeared before our old age security committee in 1950. A number of years have gone by since then, and it seems to me that the position of the welfare council of greater Winnipeg and of the Canadian Welfare Council is well taken, that the time has come for a review of this matter and for research into this whole question.
That was the point of the questions to which I have already referred, namely that in my view research into whether or not old age pensioners are eating adequately is just as important as some of the other fields of research which it is suggested should be undertaken. This indeed would be research into how old people are able to keep alive on $40 a month. I am satisfied that if such research were carried on it would be ascertained that it is impossible to live on that amount of money. I am sure that any objective group carrying on such research would come back with the recommendation that there should be an increase in the amount of the old age pension.
I have already referred to this excellent report prepared by the welfare council of

Committee on Atomic Energy greater Winnipeg. I have indicated that on page 41 is the suggestion that the government's $40 per month program should be reviewed. I should like hon. members also to look at page 26 of the report, where it is stated that so far as Winnipeg is concerned, this body of researchers has discovered that for couples and single persons over 70, median incomes are only slightly greater than the old age pension. The report states:
This means that half of the aged-at 70 or over- depend almost entirely on the pension for cash income. It is also clear that the pension in itself is not sufficient for purchase of the necessities of life in an urban community.
I am not going to read further except to indicate that the very next paragraph on page 26 is entitled " 'Life On Forty' Is No Pleasure." The paragraph goes on to make it crystal clear that trying to live on $1.31 per day is an utterly impossible task. This report, I might point out, is based on research into all the activities of older people in the Winnipeg area, how they manage to eat, their medical problems, the kind of housing conditions under which they live, and so on. There is a mass of information but it is, of course, related only to older people in the city of Winnipeg. If research like that could be made into the lives of old age pensioners in various cities across Canada there would be amassed evidence that even the Minister of National Health and Welfare could not resist, in fact, evidence I believe he would be glad to use in a campaign within the cabinet for an increase in the amount of pension to at least $60 or $65 a month.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that Your Honour was not in the chair when I took the floor, and you may wonder just what is before the house. When you left the chair you thought we were discussing a motion having to do with research into atomic energy and matters of that kind but, as no doubt your assistant deputy has pointed out to you, the debate has taken a rather wide turn while you have been out of the chamber.
I do not object to the wide turn it has taken. In fact I welcome it; that is obvious. It was made particularly wide by the very interesting speech made by the hon. member for Northumberland, who expressed pride, in which we all share, in what has been done in this country in the way of research that has been carried on under the Department of National Health and Welfare, or by means of grants made under the direction of that department. I do not wish to detract by one iota from what the hon. member for Northumberland said. Rather I suggest we go further. The Department of National Health and Welfare, which is so proud of the research that has been done and the progress that has


been made on the basis of that research, should initiate further research into the question of how old people are getting along on $40 a month.

subtopic: ATOMIC IRRADIATION
ATOMIC IRRADIATION
speechtext:
1.	Is atomic irradiation being used by Canadian agricultural scientists in the development ol new varieties of crops?
2.	If so, what is the type of equipment and the approximate cost of its use by federal employees?
3.	What improvements in various kinds of crops have been obtained by this method?
4.	To what extent, if any, does atomic irradiation increase the number of mutations that plant breeders can obtain in a given period of time?
Answer by: Mr. Gardiner:
1.	No, but X-ray irradiation is being used by the experimental farms service in cooperation with the national research council. Some work is also being done at the University of Saskatchewan.
2.	The experimental farms service has, up to the present time, not purchased any special equipment for either X-ray or atomic radiation work.
The X-ray irradiation equipment at the national research council has been made available for our work. The approximate cost of this equipment is $25,000.
3.	No productions of economic value have been developed in Canada. However, this program of work has not been active for a sufficient time to evaluate this method from the standpoint of the production of useful mutations in various species and varieties of farm crops.
4.	Genes in a given plant species mutate at a very low rate under natural conditions. Irradiation greatly speeds up mutation rates. Thus, in barley the mutant gene influencing strength of stems occurs with a frequency of two per 1,000 spike progenies, following an irradiation of 10,000 r-units. The rate of mutations here has increased manyfold over that occurring under natural conditions.
In the case of genes controlling rust resistance in oats, a tenfold increase in the mutation rate of irradiated material over natural rate has been brought about with the proper dosage of irradiation.
